newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds strengthen on back of firmer UK gilts.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds strengthen on back of firmer UK gilts.

text.p: Irish bonds strengthened, particularly in the longer paper, in late trade on Tuesday on the back of firmer gilts, after a 25 basis points UK rate rise and far-reaching reforms to the Bank of England, dealers said.

UK Chancellor Gordon Brown raised interest rates to 6.25 percent to prevent inflation getting out of hand and also announced that the Bank of England is to have independence over setting interest rates.
"Basically what has happened is UK gilts have been doing well on the back of stronger sterling since the rise in interest rates and the reform of the Bank of England was announced," one dealer said.

"People who were short of Irish and long in the UK have been taking money out of the UK and putting it into Ireland. That is a reverse of what we saw happen last week. The short-end has been helped by the Irish Central Bank intervening and fixing the one-month money rate at 6.125," the dealer said.

By 1523 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up eight pence from Friday's close at 101.83 to yield 6.00 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was up 40 pence at 109.00 to yield 6.66 percent.
Dealers said Ireland was likely to continue to follow the UK's lead over the next few days.

"If sterling continues to go up over the next few days then of course people will be looking at the whole currency and interest rates situation in Ireland again," one dealer said. -- Damien Lynch, Dublin newsroom +353 1 661 3377
